strengths: Significance: Converting predictions into two cardinality constraints provides a simple, potentially useful interface to commercial MIP solvers. The focus on repeatedly solving related instances is practically relevant.

Soundness: Algorithm 1 partitions the feasible region exhaustively. Solving all four regions preserves global optimality independently of prediction accuracy, giving the framework a valid exact-solution fallback.

Evaluation: Experiments cover knapsack, set covering, and unit commitment with both Gurobi and COPT under several heuristic settings. Figure 1 reports substantial improvements in incumbent finding, particularly for set covering, including with default solver heuristics.

Presentation, limitations, and ethics: The overall organization makes the method accessible. Remark 6 acknowledges the unrealistic exact-posterior assumption, and Section 4.4 discusses infeasible restrictions. These acknowledgments are appropriate. The described synthetic and public benchmark experiments raise no apparent material research-ethics concerns.
weaknesses: Soundness: The central concentration argument is not established. Appendix B.1 moves from an integral of a product to a product of integrals in equations (3)–(4); independent training datasets do not justify this factorization when errors share the same test instance. Separately, Theorem 2 applies concentration to prediction-selected sets U and L using unconditional accuracies. A3 does not justify this selection step: with an all-zero optimal vector and independent occasional false-positive predictions, marginal accuracy can be high while every variable selected into U is misclassified.

Soundness of the practical justification: Theorem 3 requires exact conditional means and suitable independence, neither of which is validated for the fitted logistic models or LP-based surrogates. No calibration or empirical optimal-solution coverage analysis connects these assumptions to the implementation. Moreover, some SCP training labels are generated with a permitted 10% optimality gap, whereas the theoretical setup assumes optimal labels.

Soundness of pruning: Section 3.2 states that when the preferred region excludes all optimal solutions, all complementary regions become infeasible after adding the incumbent objective cutoff. This is reversed: a complementary region must contain an optimum satisfying that cutoff. Even when the preferred region contains an optimum, inexpensive LP pruning does not follow automatically. Exhaustive branching remains valid, but this claimed justification requires correction.

Strength of empirical evidence: Section 4.2 measures time to reach PreMIO's own 120-second incumbent, leaving solution quality at common time budgets insufficiently characterized. SCUC has only five test instances per configuration, and variability across repeated runs is unreported. Section 4.4 excludes infeasible PreMIO restrictions and joint timeouts, retaining 57 of 132 MIPLIB instances. The reported 16% improvement consequently establishes performance only on this selected subset; evaluation across all instances, including fallback costs and solution gaps, is needed.

Originality: The construction closely relates to prediction-distance restrictions [11] and local branching [12]. There are no direct comparisons with these methods or neural diving [25], and no ablation establishes the benefit of the concentration-derived thresholds over empirically tuned cardinality limits. The useful integration idea is discernible, but its incremental contribution is insufficiently isolated.

Reproducibility: The manuscript provides no code link, precise solver versions, random seeds, or sufficient model-training details. Reported statistics also need reconciliation: Table 3 contains 30 entries, including a duplicated blp-ar98, despite describing 57 instances. Applying the stated shift-10 geometric-mean formula to Table 1's left panel gives approximately 36.6 and 32.1 seconds, rather than the reported 28.7 and 25.8.

Presentation and implementation clarity: Appendix D defines its purported accuracy measures using misclassification indicators and then recommends maximizing them. It also selects tau approximately 0.1 despite specifying tau in [0.5, 1). These contradictions directly affect the advertised hyperparameter-selection procedure and require substantive clarification.
